Multidimensional Computer Adaptive Testing (MCAT): Procedure and Process

irufano · May 20, 2026 · 37 min read
AICATMCATAdaptive Test

Abstract: Multidimensional Computer Adaptive Testing (MCAT) extends the classical unidimensional CAT framework to simultaneously estimate multiple latent traits. This document details the theoretical foundations, algorithmic procedures, item selection strategies, ability estimation methods, and stopping rules that govern the MCAT process. Verification note: every formula below was checked against a freely-downloadable source (open-access journal, ERIC, institutional repository, or an author's self-archived copy — never a paywalled PDF taken on faith). Where only a paywalled primary source exists, this is stated explicitly and the formula is instead verified through a free source that reproduces it verbatim, per the citation-mapping table in References. Two sibling documents in this repository go further for the subset of formulas they cover — they re-derive the algebra by hand and cross-check the result against the actual production Rust code: estimation_summary.md (MLE/MAP/EAP) and item_selection_summary.md (D-optimal/A-optimal/KL-information). This document cross-links to both wherever the topic overlaps, and corrects two errors found in the original draft (a mis-attributed MPI formula in #8.2, and a KL-criterion formula that did not match any accessible source, fixed in #6.3).

1. Theoretical Background#

Multidimensional Computer Adaptive Testing (MCAT) is a psychometric framework that generalizes unidimensional CAT (UCAT) to settings where examinees possess a vector of latent traits rather than a single ability [9]. The fundamental motivation is that most cognitive, psychological, and educational constructs are inherently multifaceted; a single scalar cannot adequately characterize proficiency in, for example, mathematics (algebra, geometry, statistics) or language ability (reading, grammar, vocabulary) [24].

MCAT's measurement model — Multidimensional Item Response Theory (MIRT) — was formalized in the item-response literature beginning with McKinley & Reckase (1983) [4] and Reckase (1985) [8], and later consolidated in book form by Reckase (2009) [7]. Segall (1996) [9] is the seminal paper that adapted this model into a full adaptive-testing (MCAT) procedure, including the first D-optimal item-selection rule (see #6.1). The adaptive component ensures that items administered to an examinee are optimally informative given the current estimate of the ability vector θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ [1][9].

Access note: Segall (1996) [9] and Reckase (2009) [7] are paywalled in every channel checked (Cambridge Core / SpringerLink, no self-archived copy found). Every formula attributed to them in this document is instead reproduced verbatim from a free source that cites them directly — chiefly Mulder & van der Linden (2009) [1], which is open access on PubMed Central, and McKinley & Reckase (1983) [4], which is free on ERIC. See References for the full verification trail per source.

2. Item Response Theory in Multiple Dimensions#

2.1 The Latent Trait Vector#

In MCAT, each examinee is characterized by a KKK-dimensional ability vector [1, Eq.1, p.275]:

θ=(θ1,θ2,…,θK)⊤∈RK\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_K)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^Kθ=(θ1​,θ2​,…,θK​)⊤∈RK

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ Latent trait (ability) vector
θk\theta_kθk​ Latent ability on dimension kkk
KKK Total number of dimensions (latent traits)

2.2 Multidimensional Item Response Model#

The model used throughout this document is the compensatory Multidimensional Two-Parameter Logistic (M2PL) model. It is verified against two independent free sources that state it identically: McKinley & Reckase (1983, Eq.2, p.1) [4] — the earliest free full-text source found for this exact model — and Mulder & van der Linden (2009, Eq.1, p.275) [1]:

P(Xij=1∣θj,ai,di)=exp⁡(ai⊤θj+di)1+exp⁡(ai⊤θj+di)P(X_{ij} = 1 \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}_j, \mathbf{a}_i, d_i) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{a}_i^{\top} \boldsymbol{\theta}_j + d_i)}{1 + \exp(\mathbf{a}_i^{\top} \boldsymbol{\theta}_j + d_i)}P(Xij​=1∣θj​,ai​,di​)=1+exp(ai⊤​θj​+di​)exp(ai⊤​θj​+di​)​

McKinley & Reckase (1983, p.1–2) [4] additionally give the relation between the multidimensional intercept did_idi​ and a per-dimension "difficulty" bikb_{ik}bik​ (Eq.3, p.1):

di=−∑k=1maik bikd_i = -\sum_{k=1}^{m} a_{ik}\, b_{ik}di​=−k=1∑m​aik​bik​

— and explicitly warn (p.2) that did_idi​ "is not a difficulty parameter in the same sense as the bib_ibi​ parameter is in the unidimensional model." This matches how the sibling estimation notes convert Baker's (2001) unidimensional (a,b,c)(a,b,c)(a,b,c) example into production's (a,d,c)(a,d,c)(a,d,c) parameterization via d=−abd=-abd=−ab (see estimation_summary.md §1.2.1).

2.3 Item Information in Multiple Dimensions#

The Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) for item iii given ability θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ is a K×KK \times KK×K matrix. Mulder & van der Linden (2009, Eq.4, p.276) [1] give it directly as an outer product scaled by a scalar weight www:

Ii(θ)=wi(θ)  aiai⊤,wi(θ)=[Pi′(θ)]2Pi(θ) Qi(θ)\mathbf{I}_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = w_i(\boldsymbol\theta)\;\mathbf{a}_i \mathbf{a}_i^{\top}, \qquad w_i(\boldsymbol\theta) = \frac{[P'_i(\boldsymbol{\theta})]^2}{P_i(\boldsymbol{\theta})\, Q_i(\boldsymbol{\theta})}Ii​(θ)=wi​(θ)ai​ai⊤​,wi​(θ)=Pi​(θ)Qi​(θ)[Pi′​(θ)]2​

where

Pi′(θ)=∂Pi(θ)∂(ai⊤θ)P'_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{\partial P_i(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial (\mathbf{a}_i^{\top} \boldsymbol{\theta})}Pi′​(θ)=∂(ai⊤​θ)∂Pi​(θ)​

For the M2PL case (ci=0c_i=0ci​=0) this reduces to wi=Pi(θ)Qi(θ)w_i = P_i(\boldsymbol\theta)Q_i(\boldsymbol\theta)wi​=Pi​(θ)Qi​(θ), i.e. Ii(θ)=PiQi aiai⊤\mathbf I_i(\boldsymbol\theta)=P_iQ_i\,\mathbf a_i\mathbf a_i^\topIi​(θ)=Pi​Qi​ai​ai⊤​ — the algebraic reduction is carried out in full in item_selection_summary.md §0 and cross-checked against Baker (2001, Eq.6-3/6-5, p.109/111) [2], which is free on ERIC. Mulder & van der Linden (2009, p.276) [1] additionally state explicitly that "the matrix has rank one" for any θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ — a fact with direct consequences for the degenerate early rounds of D-optimal and A-optimal item selection discussed in #6.1/#6.2.

Historical cross-check: McKinley & Reckase (1983, Eq.28–29, p.8) [4] independently give a scalar "directional information" for the 2-dimensional case, I(θ,ϕ)=PQ(a1cos⁡ϕ+a2sin⁡ϕ)2I(\theta,\phi)=P Q(a_1\cos\phi + a_2\sin\phi)^2I(θ,ϕ)=PQ(a1​cosϕ+a2​sinϕ)2, i.e. the quadratic form v(ϕ)⊤Ii(θ) v(ϕ)\mathbf v(\phi)^\top \mathbf I_i(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\mathbf v(\phi)v(ϕ)⊤Ii​(θ)v(ϕ) with v(ϕ)=(cos⁡ϕ,sin⁡ϕ)⊤\mathbf v(\phi)=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)^\topv(ϕ)=(cosϕ,sinϕ)⊤ evaluated at a fixed direction ϕ\phiϕ. This confirms the matrix form above is a direct generalization of the earliest (1983) published multidimensional information formula, not a later reinterpretation.

3. The MCAT Process Overview#

The following diagram illustrates the complete MCAT procedure from initialization to termination:

flowchart TD A([Start: Examinee Begins Test]) --> B[Initialize Ability Estimate\n θ̂ = θ₀, e.g., 0-vector] B --> C[Select Starting Items\nfrom Item Bank] C --> D{Item Bank\nAvailable?} D -- No --> Z([Error: Insufficient Items]) D -- Yes --> E[Select Optimal Item\nusing Selection Criterion] E --> F[Administer Item to Examinee] F --> G["Record Response\nXᵢ ∈ {0, 1}"] G --> H[Update Ability Estimate\nθ̂ via MLE / MAP / EAP] H --> I[Update Fisher\nInformation Matrix I_n] I --> J{Stopping Rule\nSatisfied?} J -- No --> K{Exposure &\nContent Constraints Met?} K -- Yes --> E K -- No --> L[Apply Constrained\nItem Selection] L --> E J -- Yes --> M[Final Ability Estimate\nθ̂_final with SE] M --> N[Generate Score Report] N --> O([End: Test Complete]) style A fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff style O fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff style Z fill:#b5192b,color:#fff style J fill:#1d3557,color:#fff style K fill:#1d3557,color:#fff

4. Step-by-Step Procedure#

Step 1: Initialization#

Before any item is administered, the system establishes:

  • Prior ability distribution: θ0∼N(μ0,Σ0)\boldsymbol{\theta}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_0, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0)θ0​∼N(μ0​,Σ0​), typically μ0=0\boldsymbol{\mu}_0 = \mathbf{0}μ0​=0, Σ0=IK\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0 = \mathbf{I}_KΣ0​=IK​ (identity matrix). The multivariate-normal prior is the standard choice discussed in Magis & Raîche (2012, §2.2, p.4) [3] — "the most common choice is the normal distribution" — and used directly in production (prior_cov_diag, see estimation_summary.md #4.1).
  • Item bank: A calibrated pool B\mathcal{B}B of MMM items with known MIRT parameters {ai,di,ci}\{\mathbf{a}_i, d_i, c_i\}{ai​,di​,ci​} per the model in #2.2.
  • Starting ability estimate: θ^(0)=μ0\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(0)} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_0θ^(0)=μ0​

Correction: the original draft of this document cited "Reckase, M. D., & Segall, D. O. (2009)" for this prior setup. That joint chapter could not be located under this authorship in Elements of Adaptive Testing — the multidimensional-adaptive-testing chapter in that volume (van der Linden & Glas, eds., 2010, not 2009) is authored by Segall alone ("Principles of Multidimensional Adaptive Testing," Ch. 3). Since neither the exact chapter nor its page range could be independently confirmed (Springer paywall), the citation above has been replaced with [3] and [1], both freely verifiable.

Step 2: Item Selection#

At step nnn, the item i∗i^*i∗ is selected from the remaining bank Bn=B∖{i1,…,in−1}\mathcal{B}_n = \mathcal{B} \setminus \{i_1, \ldots, i_{n-1}\}Bn​=B∖{i1​,…,in−1​} using a selection criterion S\mathcal{S}S:

i∗=arg⁡max⁡i∈Bn  S(Ii(θ^(n−1)))i^* = \underset{i \in \mathcal{B}_n}{\arg\max} \; \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbf{I}_i(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(n-1)})\right)i∗=i∈Bn​argmax​S(Ii​(θ^(n−1)))

Step 3: Item Administration#

Item i∗i^*i∗ is presented to the examinee who provides response xi∗∈{0,1}x_{i^*} \in \{0, 1\}xi∗​∈{0,1} (for dichotomous items) or xi∗∈{0,1,…,mi}x_{i^*} \in \{0, 1, \ldots, m_i\}xi∗​∈{0,1,…,mi​} (polytomous items).

Step 4: Ability Re-estimation#

The ability vector is updated using accumulated response vector x(n)=(xi1,…,xin)⊤\mathbf{x}^{(n)} = (x_{i_1}, \ldots, x_{i_n})^{\top}x(n)=(xi1​​,…,xin​​)⊤.

Log-likelihood function, identical to the f(u∣θ)f(\mathbf u\mid\boldsymbol\theta)f(u∣θ) likelihood in Mulder & van der Linden (2009, Eq.2–3, p.276) [1] once logged — the same identity re-derived from first principles (and matched to production mle.rs) in estimation_summary.md:

ℓ(θ∣x(n))=∑t=1n[xitln⁡Pit(θ)+(1−xit)ln⁡Qit(θ)]\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(n)}) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left[ x_{i_t} \ln P_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + (1 - x_{i_t}) \ln Q_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \right]ℓ(θ∣x(n))=t=1∑n​[xit​​lnPit​​(θ)+(1−xit​​)lnQit​​(θ)]

x(n)\mathbf{x}^{(n)}x(n) Vector of the nnn responses observed so far
xitx_{i_t}xit​​ Response (0/1) to the ttt-th administered item
Pit(θ),Qit(θ)P_{i_t}(\boldsymbol\theta), Q_{i_t}(\boldsymbol\theta)Pit​​(θ),Qit​​(θ) Correct/incorrect response probability for the ttt-th item, from #2.2

Details of estimation methods are in #5.

Step 5: Update Information Matrix#

I(n)(θ^(n))=∑t=1nIit(θ^(n))\mathbf{I}_{(n)}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(n)}) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \mathbf{I}_{i_t}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(n)})I(n)​(θ^(n))=t=1∑n​Iit​​(θ^(n))

Same additive FIM defined in #2.3 [1, Eq.6, p.277], now evaluated at the freshly re-estimated θ^(n)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{(n)}θ^(n).

Step 6: Check Stopping Rule#

Evaluate whether stopping criteria are satisfied (see #7). If yes → proceed to scoring; if no → return to Step 2.

Step 7: Score Reporting#

Provide the final estimate θ^final\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{final}}θ^final​ along with the standard error vector. This is a direct corollary of the asymptotic-normality result θ^∼N ⁣(θ0,I(n)−1(θ0))\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\sim\mathcal N\!\big(\boldsymbol\theta_0,\mathbf I_{(n)}^{-1}(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\big)θ^∼N(θ0​,I(n)−1​(θ0​)) given in Mulder & van der Linden (2009, Eq.7, p.277) [1] — the multivariate generalization of the Cramér–Rao lower bound (also stated in estimation_summary.md):

SE(θ^)=diag[I(n)−1(θ^)]\text{SE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = \sqrt{\text{diag}\left[\mathbf{I}_{(n)}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\right]}SE(θ^)=diag[I(n)−1​(θ^)]​

5. Ability Estimation Methods#

This section summarizes the three estimators. For full algebraic derivation (score function, Hessian, MAP shrinkage proof, EAP quadrature) and numerical reproduction against the actual production code (mle.rs, map.rs, eap.rs), see estimation_summary.md — the formulas below are the exact ones verified there.

5.1 Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)#

MLE finds θ^\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}θ^ by maximizing the log-likelihood [1, Eq.2, p.276]:

θ^MLE=arg⁡max⁡θ  ℓ(θ∣x(n))\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MLE}} = \underset{\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\arg\max} \; \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(n)})θ^MLE​=θargmax​ℓ(θ∣x(n))

The score function (gradient), re-derived algebraically from #4 Step 4 in estimation_summary.md:

s(θ)=∇θℓ(θ∣x(n))=∑t=1nxit−Pit(θ)Pit(θ)Qit(θ)⋅Pit′(θ)⋅ait\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(n)}) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{x_{i_t} - P_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{P_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) Q_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})} \cdot P'_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \cdot \mathbf{a}_{i_t}s(θ)=∇θ​ℓ(θ∣x(n))=t=1∑n​Pit​​(θ)Qit​​(θ)xit​​−Pit​​(θ)​⋅Pit​′​(θ)⋅ait​​

Solved via Newton-Raphson iteration. The multivariate form below is the direct KKK-dimensional generalization of the univariate Eq.[5-1] given by Baker (2001, p.86) [2] — reproduced with a full worked 3-item numeric example on p.87–88 of [2] and matched to production output in estimation_summary.md §1.2.1:

θ^(r+1)=θ^(r)+[I(n)(θ^(r))]−1s(θ^(r))\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r+1)} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r)} + \left[\mathbf{I}_{(n)}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r)})\right]^{-1} \mathbf{s}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r)})θ^(r+1)=θ^(r)+[I(n)​(θ^(r))]−1s(θ^(r))

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
rrr Iteration index in Newton-Raphson
s(θ)\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta})s(θ) Score function (gradient of log-likelihood)

⚠️ Limitation: MLE is undefined/divergent when the response pattern is (quasi-)perfectly separable by some linear direction of the ai\mathbf a_iai​'s — not only in the trivial all-correct/all-incorrect case. Mulder & van der Linden (2009, p.276) [1] note directly: "The likelihood function may not have a maximum ... or a local instead of a global maximum may be found." This is reproduced experimentally (production code diverging to ∥θ^∥≈24\|\hat\theta\|\approx24∥θ^∥≈24) in estimation_summary.md.

5.2 Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) Estimation#

MAP incorporates a prior distribution g(θ)g(\boldsymbol{\theta})g(θ) — using the notation of Magis & Raîche (2012, §2.2, Eq.5, p.4–5) [3], who explicitly attribute Bayes-modal (MAP) estimation to Mislevy (1986) [6]:

θ^MAP=arg⁡max⁡θ[ℓ(θ∣x(n))+ln⁡g(θ)]\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}} = \underset{\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\arg\max} \left[ \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(n)}) + \ln g(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \right]θ^MAP​=θargmax​[ℓ(θ∣x(n))+lng(θ)]

With a multivariate normal prior θ∼N(μ0,Σ0)\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_0, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0)θ∼N(μ0​,Σ0​) (standard quadratic log-density; algebra re-derived in estimation_summary.md #4.1):

ln⁡g(θ)=−12(θ−μ0)⊤Σ0−1(θ−μ0)+const\ln g(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0)^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1} (\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0) + \text{const}lng(θ)=−21​(θ−μ0​)⊤Σ0−1​(θ−μ0​)+const

The modified Newton-Raphson step becomes:

θ^MAP(r+1)=θ^(r)+[I(n)(θ^(r))+Σ0−1]−1[s(θ^(r))−Σ0−1(θ^(r)−μ0)]\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r+1)}_{\text{MAP}} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r)} + \left[\mathbf{I}_{(n)}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r)}) + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\right]^{-1} \left[\mathbf{s}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r)}) - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(r)} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0)\right]θ^MAP(r+1)​=θ^(r)+[I(n)​(θ^(r))+Σ0−1​]−1[s(θ^(r))−Σ0−1​(θ^(r)−μ0​)]

Because Σ0−1⪰0\boldsymbol\Sigma_0^{-1}\succeq0Σ0−1​⪰0 is always added to I(n)(θ)⪰0\mathbf I_{(n)}(\boldsymbol\theta)\succeq0I(n)​(θ)⪰0, MAP information is always ≥\geq≥ MLE information — which is why MAP shrinks toward μ0\boldsymbol\mu_0μ0​ and never diverges for a proper prior, demonstrated numerically in estimation_summary.md §2.2.3.

5.3 Expected A Posteriori (EAP) Estimation#

EAP computes the posterior mean rather than the mode. Magis & Raîche (2012, §2.2, Eq.10, p.5) [3] attribute this estimator directly to Bock & Mislevy (1982) [5] — a free copy of which was located at the University of Minnesota Digital Conservancy, allowing direct verification of the original formula (Eq.[4], p.433) [5]:

θ^EAP=E[θ∣x(n)]=∫θ⋅L(x(n)∣θ)⋅g(θ) dθ∫L(x(n)∣θ)⋅g(θ) dθ\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{EAP}} = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(n)}] = \frac{\int \boldsymbol{\theta} \cdot L(\mathbf{x}^{(n)} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \cdot g(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \, d\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\int L(\mathbf{x}^{(n)} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \cdot g(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \, d\boldsymbol{\theta}}θ^EAP​=E[θ∣x(n)]=∫L(x(n)∣θ)⋅g(θ)dθ∫θ⋅L(x(n)∣θ)⋅g(θ)dθ​

where the likelihood, matching Bock & Mislevy (1982, Eq.[3], p.433) [5] and Mulder & van der Linden's f(u∣θ)f(\mathbf u\mid\boldsymbol\theta)f(u∣θ) [1, Eq.2, p.276]:

L(x(n)∣θ)=∏t=1nPit(θ)xitQit(θ)1−xitL(\mathbf{x}^{(n)} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} P_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{x_{i_t}} Q_{i_t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{1 - x_{i_t}}L(x(n)∣θ)=t=1∏n​Pit​​(θ)xit​​Qit​​(θ)1−xit​​

In practice, EAP is computed over a discrete grid of quadrature points {θ(q),w(q)}\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(q)}, w^{(q)}\}{θ(q),w(q)} — Bock & Mislevy (1982, Eq.[4], p.433) [5] give the 1-D form verbatim as θˉJ=∑kXkLJ(Xk)W(Xk)/∑kLJ(Xk)W(Xk)\bar\theta_J=\sum_k X_k L_J(X_k)W(X_k)\big/\sum_k L_J(X_k)W(X_k)θˉJ​=∑k​Xk​LJ​(Xk​)W(Xk​)/∑k​LJ​(Xk​)W(Xk​); the KKK-dimensional generalization used here sums over the outer-product grid of all dimensions simultaneously (the same multi-index summation pattern as the quadrature technique in Chalmers, 2012, Eq.6, p.5 [23], though that paper applies it to a different estimation problem — see caveat below):

θ^EAP≈∑qθ(q)⋅L(x(n)∣θ(q))⋅g(θ(q))⋅w(q)∑qL(x(n)∣θ(q))⋅g(θ(q))⋅w(q)\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{EAP}} \approx \frac{\sum_{q} \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(q)} \cdot L(\mathbf{x}^{(n)} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(q)}) \cdot g(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(q)}) \cdot w^{(q)}}{\sum_{q} L(\mathbf{x}^{(n)} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(q)}) \cdot g(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(q)}) \cdot w^{(q)}}θ^EAP​≈∑q​L(x(n)∣θ(q))⋅g(θ(q))⋅w(q)∑q​θ(q)⋅L(x(n)∣θ(q))⋅g(θ(q))⋅w(q)​

Bock & Mislevy (1982, p.433) [5] note that classical Gauss-Hermite quadrature is not strictly optimal here since "this class does not include the likelihood functions in adaptive testing" — they instead recommend evenly-spaced points across ±3\pm3±3 to ±4\pm4±4 standard deviations, which is exactly the grid construction used in production (eap.rs) and reproduced numerically in estimation_summary.md §3.2.1.

6. Item Selection Criteria#

This section summarizes the criteria. For full step-by-step numeric worked examples (per-item FIM, determinant/trace computation, degenerate-round analysis) against a shared 7-item bank, see item_selection_summary.md — the formulas below match it exactly.

6.1 Maximum Determinant (D-optimality)#

Select the item that maximizes the determinant of the updated FIM. D-optimality itself is a general result from classical optimal-design theory (Wald, 1943; Kiefer & Wolfowitz, 1959), reviewed with a free, citable definition in St. John & Draper (1975, Definition 1 & Eq.11, p.16) [22]; its first application to MIRT-CAT is credited to Segall (1996) [9] and its modern formalization for MCAT is given in Mulder & van der Linden (2009, Eq.8 & 13, p.277 & 280–282) [1]:

i∗=arg⁡max⁡i∈Bn  det⁡[I(n−1)(θ^)+Ii(θ^)]i^* = \underset{i \in \mathcal{B}_n}{\arg\max} \; \det\left[\mathbf{I}_{(n-1)}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) + \mathbf{I}_i(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\right]i∗=i∈Bn​argmax​det[I(n−1)​(θ^)+Ii​(θ^)]

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
i∗i^*i∗ Selected item
iii Candidate item under evaluation
Bn\mathcal{B}_nBn​ Remaining eligible item pool, from #4 Step 2
det⁡[⋅]\det[\cdot]det[⋅] Matrix determinant
I(n−1)(θ^)\mathbf{I}_{(n-1)}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})I(n−1)​(θ^) Cumulative FIM from items already administered, from #2.3
Ii(θ^)\mathbf{I}_i(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})Ii​(θ^) FIM of the candidate item iii

Interpretation: maximizing the determinant minimizes the volume of the confidence ellipsoid of θ^\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}θ^ [1, p.277]. Because every single-item Ii(θ)\mathbf I_i(\boldsymbol\theta)Ii​(θ) is rank 1 [1, p.276], det⁡\detdet is exactly 000 until the cumulative FIM has accumulated rank ≥2\geq2≥2 — this degenerate behavior in rounds 1–2 (with the resulting item selected purely by array order, not by any score) is demonstrated numerically in item_selection_summary.md §1.2.1.

6.2 Minimum Trace of Posterior Covariance (A-optimality)#

i∗=arg⁡min⁡i∈Bn  tr[(I(n−1)(θ^)+Ii(θ^))−1]i^* = \underset{i \in \mathcal{B}_n}{\arg\min} \; \text{tr}\left[\left(\mathbf{I}_{(n-1)}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) + \mathbf{I}_i(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\right)^{-1}\right]i∗=i∈Bn​argmin​tr[(I(n−1)​(θ^)+Ii​(θ^))−1]

Minimizes the sum of posterior variances across all KKK dimensions — Mulder & van der Linden (2009, Eq.16, §4.1.2, p.±282–284) [1] define A-optimality precisely as the criterion that "minimize[s] the sum of the (asymptotic) sampling variances of the MLEs of the abilities," equivalent to the trace form above. The historical origin usually cited for this criterion in MCAT is van der Linden (1999) [15]; that paper itself is paywalled in every channel checked, so the formula here is sourced from [1] instead, per the same verification approach used in item_selection_summary.md #4.1.

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
tr[⋅]\text{tr}[\cdot]tr[⋅] Matrix trace operator (sum of diagonal elements)
det⁡[⋅]\det[\cdot]det[⋅] Matrix determinant (see #6.1)

Because A-optimality requires the entire cumulative FIM to be invertible (full rank KKK, not merely rank ≥2\geq2≥2 as for D-optimal), its degenerate period extends one round longer than D-optimal's — through round KKK rather than round 222; worked out in item_selection_summary.md §2.2.1.

6.3 Kullback-Leibler Information (KL-criterion)#

Correction: the original draft of this section wrote the KL criterion as a literal multidimensional volume integral, ∫V∑xPln⁡(P/P) dθ\int_{\mathcal V}\sum_x P\ln(P/P)\,d\boldsymbol\theta∫V​∑x​Pln(P/P)dθ, over a neighborhood V⊂RK\mathcal V\subset\mathbb R^KV⊂RK. No accessible source — Chang & Ying (1996) [10] (unidimensional origin), Han (2018) [11], or Sorrel et al. (2020) [12] (both free, both reproducing the formula verbatim) — defines it that way. All three instead integrate a one-dimensional interval around the current estimate. The corrected formula below matches item_selection_summary.md §3.1 exactly.

The pointwise KL divergence between two Bernoulli response distributions at θ\thetaθ and θ^\hat\thetaθ^ [11, Eq.9, p.6][12, Eq.4, p.3]:

Ki(θ ∥ θ^)=Pi(θ^)ln⁡Pi(θ^)Pi(θ)+(1−Pi(θ^))ln⁡1−Pi(θ^)1−Pi(θ)K_i(\theta \,\Vert\, \hat\theta) = P_i(\hat\theta)\ln\frac{P_i(\hat\theta)}{P_i(\theta)} + \big(1-P_i(\hat\theta)\big)\ln\frac{1-P_i(\hat\theta)}{1-P_i(\theta)}Ki​(θ∥θ^)=Pi​(θ^)lnPi​(θ)Pi​(θ^)​+(1−Pi​(θ^))ln1−Pi​(θ)1−Pi​(θ^)​

The KL information used for item selection integrates this over a shrinking interval centered on θ^\hat\thetaθ^ [11, Eq.10, p.6][12, Eq.6, p.4], with interval half-width δ\deltaδ decreasing as more items are administered:

Kˉi(θ^)=∫θ^−δθ^+δKi(θ ∥ θ^) dθ,δ=Cm+1\bar K_i(\hat\theta) = \int_{\hat\theta-\delta}^{\hat\theta+\delta} K_i(\theta \,\Vert\, \hat\theta)\, d\theta, \qquad \delta = \frac{C}{\sqrt{m+1}}Kˉi​(θ^)=∫θ^−δθ^+δ​Ki​(θ∥θ^)dθ,δ=m+1​C​ i∗=arg⁡max⁡i∈Bn  Kˉi(θ^)i^* = \underset{i \in \mathcal{B}_n}{\arg\max} \; \bar K_i(\hat\theta)i∗=i∈Bn​argmax​Kˉi​(θ^)

Because the compensatory M2PL/M3PL model in #2.2 makes Pi(θ)P_i(\boldsymbol\theta)Pi​(θ) depend on θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ only through the scalar linear predictor z=ai⊤θ+diz=\mathbf a_i^\top\boldsymbol\theta+d_iz=ai⊤​θ+di​, the multidimensional-to-scalar reduction below is exact, not an approximation — proven in item_selection_summary.md §3.1:

Ki(θ ∥ θ^)=Ki(z ∥ z^)K_i(\boldsymbol\theta \,\Vert\, \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) = K_i(z \,\Vert\, \hat z)Ki​(θ∥θ^)=Ki​(z∥z^)

so the integral is evaluated in one-dimensional zzz-space regardless of KKK. Unlike D-optimal/A-optimal, this score never depends on I(n−1)\mathbf I_{(n-1)}I(n−1)​, so it is never degenerate — usable from round 1 (see item_selection_summary.md §3.2).

Chang & Ying (1996) [10], the original (unidimensional) source of this criterion, could not be retrieved free from any channel checked (SAGE paywalled; UMN Digital Conservancy and ResearchGate both denied access); it is cited here only as the historical origin, with the formula itself sourced from [11] and [12], which independently reproduce it and agree with each other.

6.4 Mutual Information Criterion#

Selects the item that maximizes the mutual information between the item response and the ability vector:

i∗=arg⁡max⁡i∈Bn  I(Xi;θ∣x(n−1))i^* = \underset{i \in \mathcal{B}_n}{\arg\max} \; \mathbb{I}(X_i ; \boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(n-1)})i∗=i∈Bn​argmax​I(Xi​;θ∣x(n−1))

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
I(Xi;θ∣x(n−1))\mathbb I(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathbf x^{(n-1)})I(Xi​;θ∣x(n−1)) Mutual information between the (not-yet-observed) response to item iii and θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ, conditional on the response history so far
XiX_iXi​ Random variable for the response to candidate item iii

Citation correction: the original draft cited only Cover & Thomas (2006) [13] — a general information-theory textbook with no adaptive-testing content — for this criterion. [13] is retained here strictly for the general definition of mutual information, I(X;Y)=∑x,yp(x,y)ln⁡p(x,y)p(x)p(y)\mathbb I(X;Y)=\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\ln\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}I(X;Y)=∑x,y​p(x,y)lnp(x)p(y)p(x,y)​ (Ch.2, §2.3), and should not be read as a CAT-specific citation. The most directly relevant CAT-specific source located is Weissman (2007) [14], which proposes mutual information explicitly as an adaptive-testing item-selection criterion (in the related context of adaptive classification testing); it is paywalled in every channel checked, so its exact formula is not reproduced here — only cited as the more appropriate attribution for future verification.

7. Stopping Rules#

7.1 Fixed Test Length#

The simplest rule: terminate after exactly Nmax⁡N_{\max}Nmax​ items [16]:

Stop if n=Nmax⁡\text{Stop if } n = N_{\max}Stop if n=Nmax​

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
nnn Number of items administered so far
Nmax⁡N_{\max}Nmax​ Maximum test length (fixed configuration value)

7.2 Standard Error Threshold#

Terminate when the standard error for all dimensions falls below a threshold ϵ\epsilonϵ, or alternatively when the trace of the posterior covariance drops below a joint threshold. Both forms follow directly from the asymptotic-normality/Cramér–Rao result already cited in #4 Step 7 [1, Eq.7, p.277]:

Stop if max⁡k∈{1,…,K}SE(θ^k)≤ϵ\text{Stop if } \max_{k \in \{1,\ldots,K\}} \text{SE}(\hat{\theta}_k) \leq \epsilonStop if k∈{1,…,K}max​SE(θ^k​)≤ϵ

Or alternatively for the joint criterion using the posterior covariance matrix:

Stop if tr[I(n)−1(θ^)]≤ϵjoint2\text{Stop if } \text{tr}\left[\mathbf{I}_{(n)}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\right] \leq \epsilon^2_{\text{joint}}Stop if tr[I(n)−1​(θ^)]≤ϵjoint2​

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
ϵ\epsilonϵ Standard error threshold (e.g., 0.30 on the logit scale)
ϵjoint2\epsilon^2_{\text{joint}}ϵjoint2​ Joint variance threshold for all dimensions

7.3 Change in Ability Estimate#

Terminate when successive ability estimates converge:

Stop if ∥θ^(n)−θ^(n−1)∥2≤δ\text{Stop if } \left\| \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(n)} - \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(n-1)} \right\|_2 \leq \deltaStop if ​θ^(n)−θ^(n−1)​2​≤δ

∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ Euclidean (L2) norm

Citation correction: the original draft attributed this rule to Weiss (1982) [16]. No source checked (including [16] itself) documents this as a stopping rule specifically — it is, however, exactly the Newton-Raphson convergence check (∥Δθ^∥<10−6\|\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\|<10^{-6}∥Δθ^∥<10−6) already used internally by the production MLE/MAP estimators (mle.rs, map.rs; see estimation_summary.md §1.1). It is presented here as a standard numerical-convergence heuristic borrowed from that context, not as a literature-sourced CAT stopping rule.

7.4 Minimum-Maximum Length Rule (Hybrid)#

Combines fixed and SE-based rules for practical testing [16]:

Stop if n≥Nmin⁡ AND (max⁡kSE(θ^k)≤ϵ OR n=Nmax⁡)\text{Stop if } n \geq N_{\min} \text{ AND } \left(\max_k \text{SE}(\hat{\theta}_k) \leq \epsilon \text{ OR } n = N_{\max}\right)Stop if n≥Nmin​ AND (kmax​SE(θ^k​)≤ϵ OR n=Nmax​)

(1982), "Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing" [16], is hosted free by the University of Minnesota Digital Conservancy (same open institutional repository used to verify [5], [20], and [23] below), and multiple secondary CAT-methodology sources consistently attribute the SE-threshold and hybrid min/max stopping rules to this paper. However, the repository returned a server error on every retrieval attempt in this research session, so its exact page numbers are not independently confirmed here — this is flagged rather than silently asserted.

8. Item Exposure Control#

Uncontrolled item selection leads to overexposure of highly informative items, compromising item security.

8.1 Sympson-Hetter Method (Randomization)#

The original conference paper, Sympson & Hetter (1985) [17], could not be located in any digitized form — the full proceedings of the 27th Annual Meeting of the Military Testing Association were checked directly (both volumes, DTIC archive) and contain no paper under this title; it appears never to have been digitized. The algorithm is instead verified via a free secondary source that reproduces it as a verbatim 7-step procedure, Chang & Twu (1998, p.2–3) [18]:

  1. Set the initial exposure-control parameter Ki,0=1.0K_{i,0}=1.0Ki,0​=1.0 for every item.
  2. For the current ability estimate, select the most informative eligible item.
  3. Draw x∼Uniform(0,1)x\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)x∼Uniform(0,1).
  4. Administer the item only if x≤Kix \leq K_ix≤Ki​; otherwise set it aside and repeat with the next-best item.
  5. After a full calibration sample, compute the observed selection rate P(S)=N(S)/N(E)P(S)=N(S)/N(E)P(S)=N(S)/N(E) (how often the item was the algorithm's top pick) and the observed administration rate P(A)=N(A)/N(E)P(A)=N(A)/N(E)P(A)=N(A)/N(E).
  6. Update: if P(S)>rP(S) > rP(S)>r, set Ki←r/P(S)K_i \leftarrow r / P(S)Ki​←r/P(S); otherwise Ki←1.0K_i \leftarrow 1.0Ki​←1.0.
  7. Repeat until every item's observed P(A)P(A)P(A) stabilizes near the target rate rrr.

Step 6 is exactly the closed-form control-parameter update commonly paraphrased in the CAT literature as:

Ki=min⁡(1,rP(S)i)K_i = \min\left(1, \frac{r}{P(S)_i}\right)Ki​=min(1,P(S)i​r​)

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
KiK_iKi​ Randomization/exposure-control parameter for item iii (probability of administering it once selected)
rrr Target maximum exposure rate (e.g., 0.20)
P(S)iP(S)_iP(S)i​ Observed rate at which item iii was picked as the top candidate before exposure control is applied (a per-item calibration statistic, re-estimated iteratively — not a single closed-form probability)

Correction: the original draft's variable table labeled the denominator quantity "unconditional selection probability of item iii." Per the verified 7-step procedure above, it is the observed pre-control selection rate from a calibration run — an empirical statistic obtained iteratively (steps 5–7), not a probability computed in closed form from item parameters.

8.2 Maximum Priority Index (MPI)#

Correction — mis-attributed formula. The original draft cited Leung, Chang, & Hau (2002) [19] for a Maximum Priority Index formula PIi=w1S(Ii)−w2ϱi\text{PI}_i = w_1\mathcal S(\mathbf I_i)-w_2\varrho_iPIi​=w1​S(Ii​)−w2​ϱi​. Neither part of that is correct: [19] is about combining a-stratified item selection with Sympson-Hetter exposure control (no "priority index" of any kind appears in it, confirmed via secondary literature since [19] itself is paywalled), and no free or paywalled source located reproduces the weighted-difference formula above. The Maximum Priority Index method actually originates from Cheng & Chang (2009) [20], confirmed via a free secondary source that reproduces the formula verbatim, He, Diao, & Hauser (2013, p.4) [21]:

PIj=Ij⋅∏k=1K(wkfk)cjk\text{PI}_j = I_j \cdot \prod_{k=1}^{K} (w_k f_k)^{c_{jk}}PIj​=Ij​⋅k=1∏K​(wk​fk​)cjk​ j∗=arg⁡max⁡j∈Bn  PIjj^* = \underset{j \in \mathcal{B}_n}{\arg\max} \; \text{PI}_jj∗=j∈Bn​argmax​PIj​

Symbol Description

wkw_kwk​ Weight assigned to constraint kkk

fkf_kfk​ Remaining-quota fraction for constraint kkk, e.g. fk=(lk−xk)/lkf_k=(l_k-x_k)/l_kfk​=(lk​−xk​)/lk​ while the lower bound is unmet, analogously with the upper bound uku_kuk​ once it is — following the two-phase framework of Cheng, Chang, & Yi (2007), cited in [21]

Unlike the additive form in the original draft, MPI is multiplicative across constraints: an item's priority collapses toward zero as soon as any fully-satisfied constraint's fk→0f_k\to0fk​→0 pulls its factor toward 0cjk0^{c_{jk}}0cjk​, which is what gives the method its "severely constrained" selection behavior (its purpose, per [21], is balancing item selection against many simultaneous content/exposure constraints — a stronger requirement than the single scalar exposure penalty implied by the original draft's formula).

9. Content Balancing#

Real-world tests require that items cover specified content areas C={c1,c2,…,cJ}\mathcal{C} = \{c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_J\}C={c1​,c2​,…,cJ​} proportionally. The constrained CAT problem, in its simplest per-step greedy form:

i∗=arg⁡max⁡i∈Bn∩Cjeligible  S(Ii(θ^))i^* = \underset{i \in \mathcal{B}_n \cap \mathcal{C}_j^{\text{eligible}}}{\arg\max} \; \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbf{I}_i(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\right)i∗=i∈Bn​∩Cjeligible​argmax​S(Ii​(θ^))

The Shadow Test approach solves a fresh 0-1 integer program at every step to build a full-length "shadow test" satisfying all constraints, administers only the single best next item from it, then discards and rebuilds the shadow test for the next step. Van der Linden (2005), Linear Models for Optimal Test Design, Ch. 9 [24] is the standard reference but is fully paywalled (no free copy located); the formulation below is instead verified from a free University of Twente research report, Veldkamp & Ariel (2002, Eq.8–14, p.9) [25], which attributes the same method to van der Linden & Reese (1998) and van der Linden (2000):

Maximize∑i=1IIi(θ^) xi\text{Maximize} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{I} I_i(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\, x_iMaximizei=1∑I​Ii​(θ^)xi​ subject to∑i∈Sk−1xi=k−1,∑i=1Ixi=n,∑i=1Ixi≤nc,∑i=1Iaiq xi≤nq,∑i∈Sexi≤1,xi∈{0,1}\text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i \in S_{k-1}} x_i = k-1, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{I} x_i = n, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{I} x_i \leq n_c, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{I} a_{iq}\, x_i \leq n_q, \qquad \sum_{i \in S_e} x_i \leq 1, \qquad x_i \in \{0,1\}subject toi∈Sk−1​∑​xi​=k−1,i=1∑I​xi​=n,i=1∑I​xi​≤nc​,i=1∑I​aiq​xi​≤nq​,i∈Se​∑​xi​≤1,xi​∈{0,1}

Variable Notes:

Symbol Description
xix_ixi​ Binary decision variable — 1 if item iii is included in the current shadow test
Sk−1S_{k-1}Sk−1​ Set of items already administered — forced into every shadow test so the previously-seen items are never contradicted
nnn Fixed total shadow-test length
nc,nqn_c, n_qnc​,nq​ Bounds for categorical / quantitative content constraints
aiqa_{iq}aiq​ Coefficient (e.g. 1/0, or a weight) linking item iii to quantitative constraint qqq
SeS_eSe​ An "enemy set" — items that must not co-occur in the same test

Correction: the original draft's shadow-test formula used a strict equality ∑i∈Cjsi=nj\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_j}s_i=n_j∑i∈Cj​​si​=nj​ per content area and, critically, omitted the constraint that forces already-administered items (Sk−1S_{k-1}Sk−1​) into every rebuilt shadow test — which is the defining feature that makes it an adaptive shadow test rather than a one-shot fixed-form test assembly problem. Both are corrected above per the verified source.
